text: Management of Candida species infections in critically ill patients. Lancet Infect Dis 2003; 3: 772–85. Chromoblastomycosis Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a chronic fun- gal infection that affects skin and subcutaneous tissue. It occurs worldwide but is more common in tropical and sub- tropical climates. Chromoblastomycosis may result from traumatic inoculation of a number of fungal species in- cluding Fonsecaea compacta (Phialophora compacta), F. pedrosoi (P. pedrosoi), Exophiala spinifera, E. jeanselmei, Phialophora verrucosa, Cladosporium carrionii, and Rhi- nocladiella aquaspersa. In its early stages, when lesions are small, surgical excision or cryotherapy are the treat- ments of choice, although there is some risk of dissemina- tion during surgery. Many antifungals have been tried but itraconazole and terbinafine, often in high doses and for prolonged periods, have been the most successful. Howev- er, recurrence and drug resistance has been a problem with monotherapy. Itraconazole and terbinafine (given daily on alternate weeks or daily concomitantly for up to 9 months) have been shown to be effective in selected cases of chro- moblastomycosis that were unresponsive to monotherapy. Local heat treatment aids healing and may be a useful ad- junct. Coccidioidomycosis Coccidioidomycosis is an infection caused by inhalation of the spores of Coccidioides immitis, a fungus found in the soil in arid and semi-desert areas mainly of North, Cen- tral, and South America. Common names for the infection include valley fever, desert fever, and desert rheumatism. In endemic areas, coccidioidomycosis is a common oppor- tunistic infection in immunocompromised patients. Antifungals 519 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) Patients with coccidioidomycosis may experience acute or chronic lung infections, meningitis, and disseminated dis- ease although many infections are subclinical. In immuno- competent individuals, acute pulmonary disease is usually mild and self-limiting and in 60% of cases resolves with- out specific chemotherapy. In some patients the infection progresses to chronic pulmonary coccidioidomycosis with granulomatous lesions, fibrosis, and cavitation. Less than 1% of patients develop acute progressive pneumonia (which is commonly fatal if untreated) or disseminated disease (usually involving the skin, bone, meninges, and joints). Severe pulmonary and disseminated infections are more likely in pregnant women, males, certain ethnic groups, diabetics, and immunocompromised patients
